rv.q: His cine-theatre can be clever but not cutting, obsessed with the reflecting mind-numbing mania of scrolling without pushing past it to more substantial revelations. In The Maids, for instance, Williams has applied a dewy contemporary sheen to Genet’s grungy French cruelty.

Even at its most heightened moments, The Maids never captures the electrifying danger that comes with witnessing either the consequences of the characters' behavior or something revolutionary being done with the theatrical form.
Williams's take on the text is superficial and easily interchangeable.
The production is cold, unable to penetrate more deeply into the sadness and emptiness of its characters' lives.
The Maids is an ideal vehicle for Williams's 'cinetheatre' approach.
Without the threat of real violence, Williams's The Maids gets stuck in its admittedly pretty surfaces.

cn.t: Williams' video-heavy adaptation of Genet's classic divides critics: some praise its timely exploration of class and mediated identity, while others find the tech-driven approach slick but superficial, with gimmickry overshadowing the play's power.
